findings.description: The EC2 instance's user_data embeds a static AWS access key ID and secret access key (AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMAAA / wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMAAAKEY) in plaintext. User data is readable from instance metadata, the console, and the API, and is stored in cleartext in Terraform state, so these long-lived credentials are exposed to any party with metadata or state access and cannot be rotated without redeploying.

The security group allows TCP/22 from 0.0.0.0/0. Combined with map_public_ip_on_launch on the subnet and the 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway, the portal_server instance is directly reachable and brute-forceable from the internet.

map_public_ip_on_launch = true causes every instance launched in this subnet, including portal_server, to receive a public IP, placing the workload directly on the internet with no network boundary and enabling direct inbound attack against its exposed services.
map_public_ip_on_launch = true causes instances launched in this subnet to be assigned public IP addresses automatically, exposing them to the internet rather than keeping them in a private tier.

The EBS volume attached to the internet-facing portal server does not set encrypted = true, so the disk and any snapshots derived from it are stored unencrypted and are readable by anyone with access to the underlying storage media or the snapshot.

The snapshot of the unencrypted portal_server_disk is created without encryption. Snapshots are shareable and copyable across accounts, so an unencrypted snapshot exposes the disk's full contents if it is ever shared or the storage layer is accessed.

The egress rule permits all protocols and all ports to 0.0.0.0/0, defeating egress filtering. An attacker who compromises the instance can exfiltrate the credentials embedded in user_data and reach arbitrary external command-and-control infrastructure.

The bucket receiving VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration. Flow log data records source/destination addresses and traffic metadata and is stored unencrypted at rest, exposing network topology and traffic patterns if the bucket is accessed.

No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is associated with this bucket and no bucket policy or ACL restricts access, so the flow log archive relies solely on account-level defaults with no guard preventing later policy or ACL changes from exposing it publicly.

The secondary ENI is created in the public subnet portal_subnet_a with a fixed private IP and no security_group_ids specified, so it attaches to the VPC default security group rather than portal_sg, bypassing the intended security group controls and expanding the attack surface.

The instance does not set metadata_options with http_tokens = "required", leaving the IMDSv1 endpoint reachable. On an internet-facing host, SSRF or application compromise can be leveraged to retrieve instance metadata credentials.
The security group allows TCP/80 from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing the web service to the entire internet with no restriction to a load balancer or trusted proxy, widening the attack surface of the instance.
The instance has no IAM instance profile attached, removing the ability to scope and rotate privileges via STS and forcing reliance on the hard-coded credentials embedded in user_data.

A default route 0.0.0.0/0 points at the internet gateway and the route table is associated with both public subnets, making the portal subnets fully internet-routable. This is intentional public-subnet design rather than an independently exploitable misconfiguration, but it is the routing that underpins the exposure of the instance and its security group.
